howItWorks.intro: The wellness score is a composite of five same-day self-report ratings, built so each dimension pulls the total in the direction that matches how a good or bad day actually feels.

rules.name: Composite Wellness Score
rules.explanation: Mood, energy, sleep quality, and social connection are summed directly; anxiety is subtracted from 11 first, so a lower anxiety rating contributes a higher number instead of a lower one. The five adjusted values (each 1–10) are divided by the maximum possible total of 50 and expressed as a percentage.

howItWorks.outro: Because every input is a same-day self-rating, the score reflects how today compares with other days you've logged — not an absolute clinical benchmark. Its real value comes from looking at a string of these numbers side by side, not any single reading.

faq.question: Is this the same as a clinical depression or anxiety screening?
faq.answer: No. Clinical tools like the PHQ-9 or GAD-7 use fixed item sets and scoring thresholds that were developed and validated specifically for screening. This calculator is a simpler self-report composite meant for personal tracking — useful for spotting your own patterns, not for diagnosing a mood or anxiety disorder. If you're consistently scoring low, or having thoughts of self-harm, please talk to a doctor or therapist rather than relying on this number.

faq.question: Why rate five things instead of just one overall mood number?
faq.answer: A single 1–10 mood rating is quick to log but tells you little about why a day was good or bad. Separating out anxiety, energy, sleep quality, and social connection lets you see which specific factor is moving alongside your mood — for a lot of people it's sleep debt, for others it's social contact, and the breakdown is more informative than the total on its own.

faq.question: Does the time of day I fill this in matter?
faq.answer: Yes, to some degree. Mood and energy both follow a rough circadian pattern — generally lower on waking and late in the evening, higher in late morning and afternoon for most people. Rating at a consistent time, or explicitly rating 'the day so far' at a fixed point each evening, keeps your scores comparable to each other, which matters more than any single day's exact number.

faq.question: How many days of tracking before patterns become meaningful?
faq.answer: Most people start seeing genuine patterns after two to four weeks of fairly consistent entries. One weekend, or even one rough week, usually isn't enough to separate a real trend from ordinary day-to-day variation — especially around something like a sleep-debt dip that resolves on its own once you catch up on rest.

faq.question: What counts as a 'good' score?
faq.answer: There isn't a universal cutoff, which is part of why this isn't a diagnostic tool. Your own baseline matters more than the absolute number — if you typically score in the 60s and a run of days drops into the 30s and stays there, that shift is the meaningful signal, not whether 34 or 58 is 'good' in some general sense.

howWeCalculate.intro: To see the five-factor formula in action, take a hypothetical week where someone logs Mood, Anxiety, Energy, Sleep quality, and Social connection every evening. Monday and Tuesday look ordinary: scores of 70 and 60. Wednesday, after two short nights in a row, Sleep quality drops to 4 and Energy to 4, and the composite falls to 44. Thursday compounds the sleep debt further — Sleep quality 3, Energy 3, Anxiety climbing to 7 — and the score bottoms out at 34, the week's low point. Friday brings partial recovery (52), and after two nights of genuinely restorative sleep over the weekend (Sleep quality 9 and then 8), Saturday and Sunday both land at 74. The week's average works out to (70+60+44+34+52+74+74) ÷ 7 ≈ 58.3 — but the average hides the real finding: the Wednesday–Thursday trough tracks almost exactly with the two worst nights of sleep that week, landing a day before the lowest mood readings. That lag is the kind of pattern a single day's number can never show you.
steps: Rate each of the five dimensions against the same reference point in your day — most people get the most comparable results by rating at a fixed time or as an end-of-day summary, since mood genuinely shifts across morning, afternoon, and evening.
Anxiety is flipped automatically (11 minus your rating) before anything is added, so you simply enter how anxious you felt — there's no need to invert it yourself.
The five adjusted values are summed and divided by 50, the maximum possible total, then multiplied by 100 to produce a 0–100 score you can compare day to day.
The calculation runs entirely in your browser against the numbers you typed in; nothing you enter is stored or transmitted, which matters for something as personal as mood data.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: This number describes a pattern in your own same-day ratings — it isn't a diagnostic instrument, carries no clinical cutoff, and can't substitute for an evaluation by a therapist or physician. Think of it as a self-reflection and tracking aid, nothing more.

whenToUse.intro: Daily mood scoring tends to be most informative in a few specific situations, rather than as a constant background metric you check without a reason.
scenarios: Starting or adjusting a medication or therapy approach, where you and a clinician want day-by-day data instead of relying on memory at a monthly appointment
Working through a stretch of poor sleep, shift work, or travel across time zones, to see how directly sleep debt is showing up in your mood and energy
Rebuilding a routine after a stressful period, to check whether exercise, social plans, or a steadier sleep schedule are actually moving your scores rather than just assuming they help
Noticing a recurring low point tied to a day of the week, a menstrual cycle phase, or a season — a few weeks of logged scores can confirm or rule out a pattern you've only half-noticed
Preparing for a therapy or psychiatry appointment, where a run of daily scores gives a clinician more to work with than a single 'I've been okay, I guess'

sections.title: What Is the Daily Mood Tracker Score Calculator?
sections.body: The Daily Mood Tracker Score Calculator is a free online tool designed for individuals seeking balance who need quick, accurate calculations in the mental health and wellness space. By entering your overall mood, anxiety level, energy level, you get instant results including wellness score, assessment. No formulas to memorize, no spreadsheets to build — just enter your numbers and get the answer in seconds. Whether you're a beginner or experienced professional, this calculator saves you time and eliminates guesswork.

sections.title: Why This Calculation Matters
sections.body: Getting wellness score right can make the difference between success and costly mistakes. In mental health and wellness, small errors compound quickly. Manual calculations are error-prone and time-consuming, especially under pressure. This calculator applies proven formulas used by individuals seeking balance worldwide, giving you confidence that your numbers are correct. Use it to support your mental well-being with precision and avoid common pitfalls that trip up beginners.

sections.title: When Should You Use This Calculator?
sections.body: This tool is most useful when you know your overall mood and need to find the right wellness score. It's also great for quick estimates before committing to a decision, and to double-check manual calculations or professional quotes, and when comparing different scenarios side by side. Bookmark this page and come back whenever you need a fast, reliable answer — the calculator is always free and requires no signup.
